subject: chemistry
title: Polymer structure
key_idea: Polymers have very large molecules made of long chains of atoms. Atoms in the chains are joined by strong covalent bonds. The intermolecular forces between the chains are relatively strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.

blocks.text: This section covers the structure of a polymer, using poly(ethene) as the example.

items.meaning: A substance of high average relative molecular mass, made up of small repeating units.
The small group of atoms that is repeated along the chain.

items: Polymers have very large molecules.
The molecules are long chains of carbon atoms.
In poly(ethene), each carbon atom is joined to other atoms by covalent bonds.
The chains are far longer than the molecules in small substances such as methane.
A polymer is made up of small repeating units and has a high relative molecular mass.
Poly(ethene) is a long chain of carbon atoms.

sections.heading: Bonding and state at room temperature

blocks.text: Two kinds of attraction matter in a polymer: the bonds inside each chain and the forces between chains.

items: Within each chain, atoms are joined by strong **covalent bonds**.
Between the chains there are **intermolecular forces**.
The covalent bonds are strong. The intermolecular forces are weak compared with covalent bonds.
Because the molecules are so large, the intermolecular forces are relatively strong compared with those between small molecules.

items.text: Polymer molecules are much larger than small molecules.
Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces.
More energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces.
The melting and boiling points are higher, so the polymer is a solid at room temperature.

items: Methane
Poly(ethene)
Covalent bonds in the chains are strong. Intermolecular forces between chains are weaker.
Polymers have larger molecules than small molecules, so stronger intermolecular forces.
Do not write about covalent bonds breaking when a polymer melts.

blocks.text: How the chains are held together decides how a polymer behaves when it is stretched or heated.

items: Polymers with no cross-links have chains held only by intermolecular forces.
The chains can slide over each other, so these polymers stretch and are flexible.
Cross-links are covalent bonds between chains. They hold the chains firmly, so the polymer is rigid and strong.
Some polymers with cross-links do not melt when heated, because too much energy is needed to overcome the cross-links.
Chains without cross-links can slide over each other, so the polymer stretches.
Cross-links are bonds between chains, so the polymer is rigid and may not melt.

checks.a: Very large molecules made of long chains of carbon atoms. The atoms in the chains are joined by strong covalent bonds.

checks.q: Explain why poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature but methane is a gas.
checks.a: Poly(ethene) has much larger molecules, so it has stronger intermolecular forces. More energy is needed to overcome them, so the melting and boiling points are higher.

checks.q: Explain why some polymers do not melt when heated.
checks.a: There are cross-links (covalent bonds) between the chains. Too much energy is needed to overcome the cross-links.

mistakes.wrong: Poly(ethene) is a solid because it has stronger covalent bonds than methane.
mistakes.right: Reference to weaker or stronger covalent bonds is not accepted. Say poly(ethene) has much larger molecules, so stronger intermolecular forces.

mistakes.wrong: Poly(ethene) melts when the covalent bonds break, which needs more energy.
mistakes.right: Reference to breaking covalent bonds is not accepted. Say more energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces.

mistakes.wrong: Melamine does not melt because it has strong intermolecular forces.
mistakes.right: Reference to intermolecular forces is not accepted. Say it contains cross-links (bonds between the polymer chains) and too much energy is needed to overcome them.

worked_example.question:
Methane is a gas at room temperature but poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature.

Explain why methane and poly(ethene) exist in different states at room temperature.
answer_points: Poly(ethene) has much larger molecules (than methane).
So it has stronger intermolecular forces.
So the intermolecular forces need more energy to break (overcome).
So the melting and boiling points are higher, and poly(ethene) is a solid.
Or, in terms of methane: much smaller molecules, weaker intermolecular forces, less energy to overcome, lower boiling point, so a gas.
worked_example.tip: Either route scores four marks. Do not refer to weaker or stronger covalent bonds, or to breaking covalent bonds.

mistakes.wrong: A polymer is a small molecule that repeats.
mistakes.right: A polymer is a substance of high average relative molecular mass made up of small repeating units. The molecule is very large.

mistakes.wrong: Poly(ethene) is a chain of hydrogen atoms.
mistakes.right: Poly(ethene) consists of large molecules containing chains of carbon atoms.

mistakes.wrong: Polymers without cross-links stretch because the polymer chains stretch.
mistakes.right: References to the polymer chains stretching are ignored. Say the chains can slide or move over each other, because the intermolecular forces are weaker than cross-links.

mistakes.wrong: A polymer that stretches is not suitable for a ruler because rulers should not be stretchy.
mistakes.right: 'Rulers should not be stretchy' is ignored. Say rulers need to be rigid, because stretching moves the scale apart and measurements are incorrect.

worked_example.question: Explain why polymers without cross-links can stretch more than polymers with cross-links.
answer_points: The polymer chains without cross-links can slide or move over each other.
The intermolecular forces holding the polymer chains together are weaker than cross-links (cross-links are covalent bonds).
worked_example.tip: An unqualified answer is taken to refer to polymers without cross-links. Do not write that the chains stretch.
